note: Ranked by value x confidence. Falsifiers were pre-registered (analyses/fresh/HYPOTHESES.md, sha256 pinned) before any number ran; 'no result' means the pre-registered test failed, and is reported as such.

findings.title: ERCOT's zone load forecasts carry a constant bias
findings.claim: ERCOT's published 7-day load forecast carries a persistent, signed, region-specific bias at the horizons that set day-ahead commitment and reserve procurement, and a bias-corrected non-negative blend of the eight published models beats every single model out of sample.

headline.sub: constant across horizons; Coast -2.4%; the system total hides it. An ensemble of ERCOT's own models cuts MAE 11.5%.

findings.who_loses: Load. A systematically over-stated forecast is procured against: it sizes ancillary/reserve buys and day-ahead commitment above need, and the cost arrives as the DAM premium and as over-procured reserves. The IMM has flagged >1 GW net-load forecast error and 2 GW of zero-value reserves; this is the load half of that, measured per zone.
findings.software_fix: ERCOT (or anyone -- every input is public) can publish a bias-corrected per-zone ensemble of its own eight models. No hardware, no market rule change: a rolling per-zone bias table plus non-negative weights, refit daily on data already posted before DAM close.

usd_scale.assumption: LOW = convergence channel: sum over hours of (ERCOT-wide 6-24 h ensemble bias MW) x (DAM - RT at HB_HUBAVG), annualised -- an upper bound on the convergence channel alone, since it credits the entire published miss to the DA/RT spread. HIGH = reserve-sizing channel: mean|bias| (990 MW) x 8760 h x $20/MW-h; the low end of that band is $8/MW-h ($69.4M/yr). The AS price is a PROXY -- NP4-188 (DAM AS MCPC) is not on disk in Phase 1. Neither channel is a cash transfer that anyone can capture in full; both are upper bounds on the resource mis-sized by the bias.

confidence.reason: 36 vintage months of ERCOT's own published forecast (2023-09..2026-08) against ERCOT's own settlement-quality load; 6,674,904 nearest-vintage errors; all SEs Newey-West HAC and all model comparisons 14-day moving-block bootstrap; the blend is fit under a strict rolling origin whose leakage bound is a tested invariant. The $ figures are the low-confidence part (AS price is a proxy band).

proxy_fields: as_price_proxy_usd_per_mw_h=$8-$20 (NP4-188 MCPC absent; proxy, replaced in Phase 2)
which of the 8 ERCOT models is 'in use' is not published in NP3-565-CD -- all 8 are treated equally and the equal-weight ensemble (model='EQW') is reported alongside
convergence channel uses HB_HUBAVG as the settlement point for the whole system

findings.title: Ancillary-service revenue collapsed
findings.claim: A MW standing in ERCOT ancillary services earned REGUP $18,747, REGDN $11,165, RRS $15,199, ECRS $17,887, NSRS $34,921 per MW-yr in 2026. The constant-composition basket (REGUP+REGDN+RRS+NSRS) moved -89% from 2023 to 2026 (90% block-bootstrap CI -94% to -77%), outside the +/-15% band the falsifier set. Normalized by in

headline.sub: $80k/MW-yr in 2026 for standing in every legacy product, CI -94 to -77%; energy overtook AS for batteries in 2024; 2026 is DAM-only (RTC era)

findings.who_loses: battery and flexible-load developers who underwrote an ancillary-services revenue stack. AS is a small, quantity-capped market -- ERCOT buys a few thousand MW of it -- so every MW of new storage bids the price down for every MW already there. The capacity-normalized fall is much larger than the price fall alone.
findings.software_fix: software cannot re-inflate a saturated capacity market, but it decides which side of the split a resource sits on: the AS leg is a per-hour product-selection problem (REGUP vs RRS vs ECRS vs NSRS, priced differently every hour) and the energy leg is a forecast problem. The measurable software value is the gap between the best-product AS bound here and a single-product standing strategy, plus the F10 capture ratio on the energy leg.

usd_scale.unit: USD per MW-yr (one MW standing 100% in the four legacy AS products)
usd_scale.assumption: The bracket is the collapse itself: LOW = 2026 ($80,033), HIGH = 2023 ($707,119), both at mean MCPC x 8760 h on the constant-composition basket. Assumes the MW is awarded every hour it offers -- an upper bound on any single resource's realized AS revenue, because AS is quantity-capped and awards are rationed. 2021 is deliberately NOT the high end: Winter Storm Uri put the basket at $6,886,947/MW-yr, a four-day event no one can underwrite.

confidence.reason: MCPC is a published primary price for every hour since 2014-05, so the prices themselves are exact. What is proxied is the QUANTITY side: award volumes per resource are not on disk, so $/MW-yr assumes a 100% award rate; and from 2025-12-05 the DAM MCPC is a financial day-ahead position rather than the binding settlement price (NP6-331 real-time AS prices are not on disk), so 2026 is a forward, not realized revenue.

proxy_fields: DAM MCPC only. From 2025-12-05 (RTC+B) the binding AS settlement price is the REAL-TIME AS clearing price (NP6-331), which is NOT on disk; the DAM MCPC continues as a financial day-ahead position and is what every 2026 number here is. Proxy, replaced in Phase 2.
$/MW-yr assumes a 100% award rate (no per-resource AS award volumes on disk).

IMM per-unit normalization uses curated/buildout.csv storage_mw (EIA-860M operating nameplate) as the AS-eligible-capacity denominator, and assumes ERCOT's AS procurement requirement is unchanged year over year.
battery AS leg assumes perfect per-hour product selection across REGUP/RRS/ECRS/NSRS (upper bound); REGDN excluded from the max (sold against charging, not discharging).
battery energy leg is F10-style perfect foresight on the four-hub constant-composition RTM average, price-rank selection without sequencing (upper bound).
AS and energy legs are computed STANDALONE and cannot both be earned on the same MW in the same hour -- the split is relative size, not a stacked total.

partial years are annualized (AS x 8760/observed hours; energy x 365/observed days). ECRS's 2023-06-10 birth year (2023) is therefore a full-year rate quoted off ~7 months of prices, and 2014 off 8 months.

findings.title: Load growth in the west is weather-independent
findings.claim: FAR_WEST weather-independent load grew ~423 MW/yr (12.0%/yr) over 2011-2026 while its cooling response grew -0.5%/yr -- not proportional, consistent with 24x7 load growth.

headline.sub: Far West weather-independent load growth, +12%/yr: the grid must be sized for energy, not peak.

findings.who_loses: Nobody is directly overcharged; the story is a planning/utilization mismatch -- capacity is provisioned and priced around peak MW, while the growth identified here is energy (all-hours) load, so peak-based buildout and rate design may be the wrong lens.
findings.software_fix: ERCOT / transmission planners: a public per-zone weather-normalized load decomposition (intercept vs. temperature-responsive) to separate 24x7 industrial growth from HVAC-driven peak growth in resource adequacy and interconnection planning.

usd_scale.assumption: intercept (weather-independent load) trend MW/yr x years observed x 8760 x zone's all-history mean DAM price at its mapped LZ/hub proxy node; a rate-times-span estimate of the $ value of accumulated 24x7 load growth, not a measured transfer. Range spans the low/high across all fitted zones (see per-zone rows in the CSV).

confidence.reason: High confidence in the regression mechanics and bootstrap CIs; medium overall because WEST has no weather station (FAR_WEST stands in), EAST is priced off HB_HUBAVG (no clean LZ match), and breakpoints are held fixed inside the bootstrap rather than re-searched.

proxy_fields: EAST priced via HB_HUBAVG (no single clean LZ match)
WEST weather-station-less: response fit only for FAR_WEST, not WEST

findings.title: The day-ahead premium is real and persistent
findings.claim: HB_HUBAVG-equivalent DAM-RT spread post-2023 averages $3.35/MWh (HAC 90% CI $1.48 to $5.23), daily-P&L Sharpe 1.44. Selling DAM / buying RT would have been a persistently profitable, positive-Sharpe carry trade even after 2023's market redesigns.

headline.sub: post-2023 day-ahead premium over real-time, Sharpe 1.44, CI $1.5-5.2

findings.who_loses: load, which pays the DAM premium to whoever is short volatility on the other side (self-committed thermal, financial desks selling DAM strips).
findings.software_fix: a public, real-time-updated DAM-RT basis/Sharpe monitor per hub would let smaller participants price the same carry trade ERCOT's largest desks already run informally.

usd_scale.assumption: gross $/MW-yr = HAC 90% CI bound on mean post-2023 DAM-RT hub-average spread x 8760 h/yr, for 1 MW fully hedged sell-DAM/buy-RT every hour; excludes collateral, CRR hedge cost and congestion (not on disk), so a real desk's net is lower than this gross figure.

confidence.reason: HAC-correct SE and a positive-Sharpe daily P&L both clear the pre-registered falsifier

proxy_fields: era breaks (Uri, ECRS 2023-06-10, RTC+B 2025-12-05) read at calendar-year granularity in the per-node table, not the exact cut date
$/MW-yr is gross: collateral, CRR hedge cost and congestion are not on disk

findings.title: Batteries capture a shrinking share of the spread
findings.claim: Storage (genmix 'Other') apparent capture ratio -- realized DAM/RTM spread over a same-cycle-count perfect-foresight benchmark -- was nan in 2021 and 0.30 in 2026 (Mann-Kendall tau=-0.60, p=0.221, trend=none; mean 0.36). Falls below the flat-and->0.7 bar the falsifier set, consistent with the spread being competed away

headline.sub: 2026 realized / perfect-foresight spread for the storage fleet; 0.36 mean, falling

findings.who_loses: existing storage owners, as more entrants compete for the same daily price spread and each MW captures a shrinking share of it.
findings.software_fix: better bidding/dispatch software cannot fix a shrinking pie -- this is a portfolio-sizing signal (marginal storage MW is worth less every year), not a software-fixable mispricing.

usd_scale.unit: USD in 2026 (realized vs perfect-foresight fleet revenue on discharged MWh)
usd_scale.assumption: low = realized $/MWh spread x that year's discharged MWh (fleet-wide, from genmix 'Other'); high = the perfect-foresight same-cycle-count benchmark spread x the same MWh -- the gap between them is the $ upper bound on 'spread left on the table', not a claim that it was capturable at that MW magnitude.

confidence.reason: genmix 'Other' is a fleet-wide proxy for net storage, not a battery-only meter (lumps in any other non-listed net generation/load); charge/discharge classification uses a fixed 200 MW noise threshold; the perfect-foresight benchmark matches interval COUNT, not MW magnitude.

proxy_fields: genmix 'Other' used as a proxy for net battery storage (not a dedicated battery meter); validated pre-2021 magnitude <1 GW (see extra.pre_2021_validation)
charge/discharge classified by a fixed 200 MW |Other| threshold
perfect-foresight benchmark matches interval count, not MW magnitude within a day

findings.title: ERS pays more than a CLR can earn, for zero hours
findings.claim: In program year 2025 a MW offered into every ERS cell earned $42,853/MW-yr (hours-weighted over 4 cells covering 8,760 h, term-average clearing price x term contract hours) for 0 hours of actual curtailment. The same MW registered as a CLR and standing in RRS every hour of 2025 earned $24,167/MW-yr at a 100% award rate

headline.sub: $42.9k vs $24.2k/MW-yr in 2025, for zero deployment hours; the 2025 CLR->ERS migration is worth $5-14M/yr

findings.who_loses: ERCOT's dispatchable-flexibility position, and every load that took on SCED dispatch. The market pays roughly twice as much for a promise as for the act: a CLR that accepts real dispatch and delivers real curtailment earns less than an ERS resource that has not been called since September 2023. The $75M ERS budget is a consumer cost with close to zero delivered energy behind it, while the fleet ERCOT can actually dispatch shrinks.
findings.software_fix: nothing a CLR's optimizer does closes a 2x gap that comes from the product design, so the honest software answer is the reverse: the value is in the ROUTING decision, not the dispatch. A tool that prices both routes cell by cell from the same primary data this module uses -- ERS Time-Period clearing prices against live AS MCPCs, per site, per term -- turns an annual registration choice into a priced one. The market-design fix (making ERS availability pay reflect delivered curtailment, or letting CLRs stack the two) is a rulebook change, and NPRR1188/1244 and RTC+B already move that way.

usd_scale.unit: USD per year of revenue gained by the MW that left CLR for ERS in 2025
usd_scale.assumption: LOW measures the MW that moved from the CLR side (254 MW of lost CLR RRS-qualified capacity); HIGH measures it from the ERS side (722 MW/h of ERS procurement growth, which includes new entrants that were never CLRs). Both multiply by the same $18,686/MW-yr gap, and both assume the ERS MW is offered into every cell of the program year.

confidence.reason: both legs are primary published prices -- ERCOT's own posted ERS clearing prices and the DAM MCPC archive -- and the conclusion survives every assumption pushed in the CLR's favour: 100% award rate, best-product-per-hour selection, and the IMM's own award share. The RRS leg reproduces the IMM's published annual DAM RRS average to within 1% (see fresh/as_prices extra.imm_price_crosscheck). What is NOT measured is the CLR's energy leg (the value of being dispatched down at a high price), which the peer's stats/clr_evidence backtests separately.

proxy_fields: CLR AS revenue assumes a 100% award rate; per-resource AS award volumes are not on disk. The award-share-adjusted line uses the IMM's FLEET ratio (78 MW of AS on 240 MW of CLR load, 2025), not an observed per-resource award. Proxy, replaced in Phase 2 from the 60-day DAM disclosure (D8).
deployment hours are a LOWER bound: some ERCOT deployment postings carry no end time and contribute zero hours here.

ERS $/MW-yr assumes a MW offered into every cell of the program year; a resource that offers into only some cells earns proportionally less, and the cells are priced very differently (DecMar25 TP1 vs weekend-morning TP7).
the CLR energy leg (self-curtailment value) is not priced here -- see the peer's curated/program_revenue.csv clr_energy rows and stats/clr_evidence.

from 2025-12-05 (RTC+B) the DAM MCPC is a financial day-ahead position rather than the binding AS settlement price (NP6-331 is not on disk), which is why the comparison year is 2025 and not the latest year.

findings.title: Tight hours stopped paying: the missing money
findings.claim: Between 2024-01-01 and 2026-07-31 the ERCOT energy market paid net load $23.6bn-$29.2bn/yr less than the 2019-01..2023-05 price law would have paid for the SAME observed net load (90% interval on the net-load-only conditioning $7.9bn-$38.4bn/yr). For a 100 MW merchant price-taker that is $476-$600/kW-yr of forgone ener

headline.sub: ex-Uri energy revenue the 2019-23 price law would have paid; fails its own placebo, so low confidence

findings.who_loses: Merchant generators and standalone storage -- the assets whose entire revenue is scarcity pricing. ERCOT's own CDR has the reserve margin going negative by 2028, and this is the price signal that is supposed to fix it.
findings.software_fix: Nobody legislates the adders back with software, but the flip side is dispatchable: if scarcity rent is administratively capped, the value of flexibility moves to ancillary services and to avoided 4CP/transmission charges, and a load that can prove firm curtailment captures it. Publishing this transport as a live index (net-load bin -> counterfactual price) is the tool.

usd_scale.unit: $/yr, all-in transfer to net load (energy channel only); low = ex-Uri training window, high = pre-registered base case
usd_scale.assumption: All-in transfer: MW = observed system net load, so this is what the energy market as a whole stopped paying, not one asset's revenue. $/kW-yr is the same gap for a 100 MW merchant unit at 100% availability (price-taker, no outages, no offer strategy). Energy channel only -- the ancillary channel is omitted, so the energy upper bound is still a lower bound on total missing money. The low end drops Winter Storm Uri from the training window; the in-era placebo is the bias floor and must be read against both.

confidence.reason: The transport identifies a conditional-price change, not its cause. The fine conditioning (hour block, month, dispatchable-output decile) absorbs fleet-mix change, the sign and size of the conditional term are stable, and tight intervals demonstrably did not stop happening. But the pre-registered base case leans on Winter Storm Uri for most of its magnitude, and the in-era placebo -- 2019-20 -> 2021-22, an interval that also spans two offer-cap changes and a 2-3x gas-price move -- returns a gap of the same order as the ex-Uri finding. Until NP6-323 adders and NP4-188 AS prices land, a counterfactual on the actual ORDC parameters (F15) is what would settle it; net load is a coarse proxy for the reserve level that actually sets the adder, and fuel cost is not conditioned on at all.

proxy_fields: ancillary channel omitted (NP4-188 AS MCPC and NP6-323 ORDC adders are not on disk); energy-channel upper bound is a total lower bound

series.label: actual vs 2019-23 price law, by year

findings.title: Price = physics + rulebook: the adder share of a scarcity print
findings.claim: Administrative price adders are pre_ecrs 55%, post_ecrs 5%, post_2024 4% of every dollar in a >=$500 hub print. 8% of post-2024 >=$500 prints would not have reached $500 on the energy price alone. Applying the recovered 2019-2023 ORDC curve to the SAME observed 2024-2025 reserve levels would have paid $99m/yr LESS in a

headline.sub: administrative ORDC/reliability adders were 55% of every dollar in a pre-ECRS scarcity print and are 4% now (90% CI 27-66% vs 1-5%); applying the old 2019-2023 ORDC curve to today's observed reserves pays $99m/yr LESS, not more, so the missing money is not the adder

findings.who_loses: Merchant generators and storage, who are paid the adder and not the energy price; and any investor who read a >=$500 print as a scarcity signal from the supply stack when most of it was an administrative term.
findings.software_fix: The decomposition is publishable in real time from data ERCOT already posts every five minutes: NP6-323 carries the adders and NP6-905 the settlement price, so a live 'how much of this print is the rulebook' gauge is a join, not a model. Any desk hedging on >=$500 prints should be marking the energy component separately, because that is the half an offer curve can respond to.

usd_scale.unit: $/yr of ORDC adder revenue the 2019-2023 curve would have paid on 2024-2025 observed reserves, over what was actually paid
usd_scale.assumption: the recovered 2019-03..2023-05 LOLP curve, priced at VOLL $5,000 (low) and $9,000 (high), applied to the observed RTOLCAP and system lambda; adder revenue is adder $/MWh x ERCOT system load, so it is the transfer to ALL generation, not to a single unit

confidence.reason: The decomposition is an identity, not a model: RTSPP = LMP + adders is ERCOT's own settlement arithmetic, and both sides are read off the archive. The counterfactual is weaker: the LOLP curve is RECOVERED from observed (reserve, adder) pairs rather than read off ERCOT's published season x hour-block (mu, sigma) tables, which are not on disk, and it is a single curve where ERCOT's is 96 of them.

proxy_fields: ORDC LOLP curve recovered from observed (RTOLCAP, RTORPA+RTOFFPA) pairs; ERCOT's published season x hour-block (mu, sigma) tables are not on disk
5-minute SCED adders averaged into the 15-minute settlement interval
adder revenue scaled by ERCOT system load (load_wz ERCOT), held flat within the hour
RTC+B (2025-12-05 ->) publishes no ORDC adder and no PRC/RTOLCAP: the RTC rows carry only the reliability deployment adder (RTRDPA) and no counterfactual
the 2019-2023 reference curve is reported with and without Winter Storm Uri (2021-02-14..21), the same window F5's own sensitivity drops
the single-normal fit to each recovered curve is a SHAPE CHECK, not a parameter estimate: see curve_shift_check, which reproduces the documented +0.50-sigma shift but not the +0.25-sigma one

series.label: share of every >=$500 print that is an administrative adder, %

findings.title: Congestion is episodic, and it is not a West Texas story
findings.claim: FALSIFIED, and the falsification is the result. The top of ERCOT's congestion ranking turns over: median year-over-year top-20 Jaccard is 0.18 by $/MW-h, 0.29 by binding hours and 0.25 by congestion rent - every reading below the pre-registered 0.30, so roughly four of every five constraints in one year's top 20 are no

headline.sub: four of five top constraints turn over each year; 27.5% of shadow value is persistent; 89% of it is outside West/Panhandle; $2.4bn/yr congestion rent at the constraint

findings.who_loses: Load and generation behind constraints that bind every summer: the congestion is predictable at the element even where node basis looks like noise, so the cost is recurring and the hedge (CRRs on the right path, or siting on the right side of the element) is knowable in advance. Whoever cannot buy that hedge pays it.
findings.software_fix: A siting/hedging tool that ranks locations by the CONSTRAINT they sit behind rather than by historical node basis: join a candidate site to the constraints whose shadow price moves its basis (the ridge map here), then score it on those constraints' recurrence, not on the node's own past. ERCOT could publish the constraint->node shift factors it already computes; today a developer has to regress them out of price data.

usd_scale.unit: USD of congestion rent at the constraint, cumulative 2021-2026 (top constraint .. all constraints)
usd_scale.assumption: congestion rent = SUM over binding 5-min intervals of shadow_price x (5/60) x limit_mw. This is the market's valuation of RELIEF AT THE CONSTRAINT - the ranking of where a transmission project would have been worth building - NOT a consumer cost and NOT consumer savings: the rent is collected by the market and largely returned as CRR revenue, and using the limit as the flow makes it an upper bound. limit_mw is present on 100% of binding rows; the limit-free ranking (shadow_mw_h, $/MW-h) is reported beside it and is the quantity the falsifier and the recurrence share are computed on.

confidence.reason: 1,962,083 binding SCED intervals over 6 years from ERCOT's own NP6-86-CD settlement-grade shadow prices; the recurrence share carries a 14-day moving-block bootstrap CI with set membership recomputed per replicate. Cross-check: 8 of ERCOT's own top-10 recent constraints (Dec 2025 report, Oct 2024-Sep 2025) appear in our top 40 by shadow $/MW-h and 9 of 10 are found anywhere in the ranking. Weaknesses: the constraint key is ERCOT's name string, so a renamed element looks like a new constraint (this biases Jaccard DOWN, against the finding); the node map is a reduced-form ridge on 2025-04->2026-08 DAM hours only, a shift-factor PROXY, not a network model.

proxy_fields: congestion_rent_usd = shadow x (5/60) x limit_mw -- rent AT the constraint, an upper bound (limit used as flow), not a consumer cost
shadow_mw_h = shadow x (5/60) -- $/MW-h, the limit-free ranking
beta_basis_per_dollar_mwh -- ridge coefficient of node DAM basis on hourly constraint intensity; a signed SHIFT-FACTOR PROXY, not a computed shift factor

region_hub -- MEASURED: sign/size of the correlation between the constraint's hourly intensity and the HB_PAN / HB_WEST DAM basis (top 300 constraints only, |corr| >= 0.1); region_name -- keyword fallback on ERCOT's station abbreviations, for the long tail; region_regress -- modal inferred zone of the ridge map's top nodes (zones from F4's zone_dispersion_nodes.csv)
gtc_flag -- STRUCTURAL: no from/to station and BASE CASE contingency, i.e. an interface-wide limit rather than a thermal rating on a named element
summer test needs >= 10 binding hours in Jun-Sep of a year whose full summer is inside the sample (summers used: [2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025])

series.label: top-20 constraint overlap, year over year

findings.title: Node decoupling from hubs is rising fast
findings.claim: Across 6 years of 15-minute nodal RTM settlement prices, the median ERCOT node's price is in its own worst 1% of intervals 88% of the times its hub is (lambda_U, q=0.99, ranks on jointly observed intervals). Every year clears the pre-registered 0.80 line (0.81-0.95) and only 0.1% of nodes decouple in every year they ar

headline.sub: median node-vs-hub tail dependence still 0.88 (falsifier fires), but the decoupled share went 0% (2021) to 16% (2025), on the same South Texas constraints as F13

findings.who_loses: Anyone who sizes a multi-site flexible-load or storage portfolio as if ERCOT nodes diversified each other. At the median node, a hub-settled hedge and the node's own settlement go wrong together in the tail, so the 'spread the sites out' answer to scarcity-price risk buys almost nothing; and where it does buy something (the persistently decoupled minority) the residual is a congestion exposure, not a hedgeable one -- CRRs settle day-ahead, this is measured in real time.
findings.software_fix: A siting and hedging tool that scores a candidate ERCOT location on its tail dependence with the hub it will be hedged against -- lambda_U at q=0.99 and 0.999, by year, with a block-bootstrap CI -- instead of on average basis. Every input is public (NP6-905-CD); the calculation is a rank transform and a conditional count. ERCOT or the IMM could publish it per settlement point at essentially zero cost, which would let a developer see before signing an interconnection agreement whether the site's worst intervals are the hub's worst intervals or its own.

usd_scale.assumption: HIGH = the MEDIAN over 6 years of the revenue transacted by one MW in the top 1% of HB_HUBAVG's 15-minute intervals (sum of price x 0.25 h, pro-rated to a full year by interval count), i.e. the whole tail exposure a flexible MW is trying to manage: $76,776/MW-yr. The median rather than the mean because the by-year range is $22,074-$788,643 and the top of it is Uri: a mean would report one week of February 2021 as a typical year. LOW = (1 - median lambda_U) x HIGH = $9,192/MW-yr, the part of that exposure that siting could in principle diversify away at the median node. Both are illustrative gross exposures, not transfers anyone captures: they ignore the node's own basis, dispatch, and the cost of being at the node in the other 99% of intervals, and they are computed on the hub price rather than on realised settlements.

confidence.reason: 5,562 node-years over 6 years (2021-2026), 197,294 15-minute intervals, 1084 nodes scored in the last year. lambda_U is a nonparametric rank statistic with no distributional assumption; the q=0.99 CI resamples whole local calendar days (500 replicates), median CI width 0.24 in the last year. The estimate is conditional on ~328 intervals per node-year at q=0.99 and ~32 at q=0.999, which is why q=0.999 is read as a direction only. The node->hub map is inferred (F4) rather than published, and 21% of node-years are benchmarked against HB_HUBAVG for want of a zone hub (4% are absent from F4's map altogether); the HB_HUBAVG column is reported for every node so that choice can be checked.

proxy_fields: node->hub is F4's INFERRED zone (zone_dispersion_nodes.csv), fitted on DAM nodal prices, not an ERCOT-published node->hub map (ERCOT does not publish one); zones without a hub (LZ_AEN/LZ_CPS/LZ_LCRA/LZ_RAYBN), unassigned nodes and nodes absent from that map benchmark against HB_HUBAVG instead -- 21% of node-years, of which 4 points are nodes F4 never saw at all
the constraint join is F13's ridge-estimated shadow-price -> basis map (constraints_nodes.csv, top-N nodes per constraint), a statistical association, not ERCOT's shift factors
q=0.999 carries a Wilson interval, not the day-block bootstrap: a full year leaves ~35 conditioning intervals, too few to resample by day
nodes are scored only in years where they are priced in >= 50% of intervals, so a node's year set changes as the fleet grows; 'persistent' is defined on scorable years

the matrix is keyed on LOCAL wall-clock time so the bootstrap's blocks are local calendar days; the four repeated intervals of the DST fall-back hour collapse onto their later (post-fall-back) copy - 4 of ~35,040 intervals a year
the Phase B anchor was DAM (0.857 median for 2026-08); this is RTM, a different market

series.label: share of nodes with tail dependence < 0.6

findings.title: Gigawatts built for fifty hours
findings.claim: ERCOT is built for a thin tail of hours: averaged across observed years, 3.3 GW of capacity is needed only in the year's top 50 hours (7.8 GW for the top 250 hours), while system-wide mean load factor in 2025 was 0.67.

headline.sub: of ERCOT exists for the top 50 hours a year

findings.who_loses: everyone who pays for the grid: N MW of capacity/transmission sized for <=50-250 h/yr is carried in rates the other 8,500+ hours a year.
findings.software_fix: demand flexibility (shed/shift load away from the top-N hours) or storage that discharges into them substitutes for physical capacity headroom -- this is the utilization thesis the whole scan is testing.

usd_scale.assumption: illustrative capacity-cost bound only: mean top-250-hour headroom GW x an industry peaker-capacity cost range of $70-$130/kW-yr; the cost range is NOT sourced from ERCOT data on disk (no CDR/resource-adequacy cost curve is in the panel) and is a labelled proxy.

confidence.reason: framing module, purely descriptive off load_wz + genmix; no model fit or hypothesis test to fail. Confidence is in the arithmetic, not in the (deferred) weather-normalized shape of the tail.

proxy_fields: weather_normalization: NOT applied (F9 out of scope for this build) -- top-N-hour tail mixes genuine thinning with 2011/2023 heat and Uri outlier years
usd_scale: illustrative peaker-capacity cost range, not sourced from on-disk data
net_load headroom (2012-): wind/solar matched at exact 15-min instant to the hourly grid; pre-2013-01-01 missing solar filled with 0 (bounded, <=76 MW nameplate; see build/netload.py)

findings.title: ERCOT's own forecast miss marks the expensive intervals
findings.claim: ERCOT's most expensive real-time intervals are concentrated in the hours ERCOT's own day-ahead forecast gets wrong: spike probability and the DAM-RT spread both rise monotonically across trailing deciles of that miss. The decile *edges* use only trailing data, but the realised miss is an ex-post variable, so this is an

headline.sub: P(>=$500) in ERCOT's most over-forecast decile; the ex-ante signal (model disagreement) carries 2.9x

findings.who_loses: Load, and any load-serving entity hedging on the day-ahead price alone. Every input is already public and free, yet nobody publishes the disagreement measure in a usable form, so flexible load that could have pre-positioned out of the flagged hours does not -- and pays for those hours twice, once in the real-time print and once in the day-ahead premium charged for bearing exactly this risk (F3).
findings.software_fix: Publish the trailing decile of cross-model disagreement in ERCOT's own posted forecast as a live public index -- a ten-line calculation on one public feed, available the moment the vintage posts -- so demand response, a battery or a curtailable data centre can pre-position before DAM close instead of reacting to the print. The ex-post error decile is the same index scored after the fact, and is what tells ERCOT which of its own misses are the expensive ones to fix (F2).

usd_scale.assumption: LOW = the 23 spike intervals/yr that fall in the flagged extreme decile x 0.25 h x the $500 threshold price -- a floor, since it prices every spike at the threshold. HIGH prices the same intervals at their observed mean of $2,714/MWh. Both assume a MW of load that actually avoids every flagged interval and none of the others; neither is a transfer anyone captures in full, and neither nets out the cost of being wrong on the 99.3% of flagged intervals that do not spike. Both are computed on the EX-POST decile, so they are a ceiling on what the ex-ante disagreement index could deliver, not a realisable revenue.

confidence.reason: 97,536 15-minute intervals matched to 24,384 forecast hours over 2.9 years; deciles cut strictly on trailing data; CIs are 14-day moving-block bootstrap on the decile curve itself, not on ten independent proportions. Medium rather than high for three reasons: the vintage archive starts 2023-09, which is only two full summers; the >=$500 base rate is thin (a few hundred intervals in the whole sample), so the extreme-decile probability rests on tens of events; and the direction runs through OVER-forecast hours, which is consistent with reverse causation -- price-responsive and curtailable load leaves in a scarcity hour, so actual comes in under ERCOT's forecast *because* the price spiked. Read the ex-post table as co-occurrence, not causation.

proxy_fields: HB_HUBAVG stands in for a system-wide real-time price; nodal RTM (NP6-905) is absent in Phase 1 (proxy, replaced in Phase 2)
the day-ahead system forecast error is the equal-weight ensemble of all 8 published ERCOT models -- which model ERCOT acts on is not published in NP3-565-CD
the signed/absolute error deciles are EX-POST (the error needs the settled actual); only the model-disagreement deciles are available before DAM close

no reserve-margin or outage regressor is available in Phase 1 (PRC and NP6-323 adders absent), so the ex-post lift is co-occurrence and is not decomposed into 'the miss caused the spike' vs 'the spike caused the miss' (proxy, revisited in Phase 2 with F15's adders)

findings.title: The Panhandle pays you to consume
findings.claim: HB_PAN priced at or below $0 for 1213 h in 2026 (2020: 2298 h), 2.46x the mean of HB_WEST/LZ_WEST over 2020-2025. That clears the 1.5x band -- Panhandle is distinctly more paid-to-consume than the rest of West, consistent with a local (transmission-congestion / stranded-wind) signature on top of any system-wide oversup

headline.sub: paid to consume at HB_PAN in 2026; 2.5x the other West points, so it is local

findings.who_loses: wind generators interconnected in the Panhandle, paid negative prices for output that cannot get out; who gains is anything that can consume there flexibly (interruptible load, storage) and collect the negative price.
findings.software_fix: curtailment-aware or price-following load siting/dispatch software in the Panhandle captures the negative-price hours directly instead of letting them go to waste as destroyed wind revenue.

usd_scale.assumption: upper bound only: system-wide (not Panhandle-only) wind MW x |HB_PAN price| summed over HB_PAN's negative-price 15-min intervals; no node-level Panhandle wind MW is on disk in this pass (proxy, replaced when the nodal wind-node parse lands).

confidence.reason: descriptive count + a documented falsifier on directly observed HB_PAN and West-hub/zone RTM prices; the only proxy is the system-wide wind MW used for the $ upper bound.

findings.title: Are the 2003 load zones stale?
findings.claim: Tested and not supported as a system-wide claim: on 17 months of hourly all-node DAM the intra-zone cross-node sd is only 0.40x the inter-zone sd at the median zone, and just 1 of 8 zones (LZ_WEST, ratio 1.28, CI 1.17-1.42) clear 1 with a weekly-block CI. Intra-zone dispersion is real but concentrated in the west and n

headline.sub: the only zone where within-zone dispersion beats between-zone; system-wide 0.40, so no result

findings.who_loses: Load and hedgers inside a zone: the zonal settlement price averages a spread its customers cannot see, hedge or site against. No load buses are in this dataset, so the transfer itself is not identified here.
findings.software_fix: ERCOT/PUCT redrawing zones on measured correlation rather than 2003 geography; in the meantime a public node-to-zone map and per-node basis feed lets siting and hedging see the dispersion the zone price hides.

Lower bound is 0: `dam_spp_nodes` has no load buses, so no transfer is identified -- load settles at the zone price by design, and this gap is an accounting spread, illustrative only, DAM only, never annualised to real time.

findings.title: The evening ramp is the new peak
findings.claim: Evening (18-21h) net-load ramp averaged -1.24 GW/h in 2011 vs 1.97 GW/h in 2026 (Mann-Kendall tau=+0.33, p=0.079, trend=none); the 18-21h window's share of the year's log-truncated price variance went from 0.10 to 0.16 (tau=+0.38, p=0.043, trend=increasing). At least one leg does not show a significant rising trend, so

headline.sub: evening net-load ramp in 2026, from -1.2 in 2011; misses the pre-registered bar (p=0.079)

findings.who_loses: no direct loser priced here; this is a structural/timing finding that feeds F1 (utilization) -- capacity built for peak MW is increasingly used to serve a 3-hour ramp, not a flat peak.
findings.software_fix: ramp-aware dispatch/forecast software (batteries pre-charged ahead of the ramp, flexible load pre-cooling/pre-processing before 18:00) substitutes for physical fast-ramp capacity.

usd_scale.assumption: no $ figure computed for this module -- F7 is a structural/timing finding (GW/h and variance share), not a mispricing claim; usd_scale intentionally left unset (NaN) rather than fabricated.

confidence.reason: ramp and price-variance series are computed directly from genmix/RTM with no proxy; confidence is capped at medium because the ramp-predictability number is a naive persistence proxy, not the real ERCOT-forecast + solar-forecast hybrid the spec describes (NP4-745 is absent from disk in this pass).

proxy_fields: ramp predictability is a naive yesterday-predicts-today persistence upper bound, NOT the real ERCOT load forecast + synthetic solar hybrid the spec describes (NP4-745 solar forecast absent from disk); a real forecast-based number would likely score higher than this proxy

findings.title: A public tightness index vs ERCOT Watches
findings.claim: A mechanical net-load-slack index, calibrated rolling-origin (Y-1 -> Y) over 2021-2026, covers 43% of $1000+ price intervals (Watch/EEA: 32%) at a 75% episode false-alarm rate (Watch: 32%), with a median lead time of 3.8h.

headline.sub: of >=$1,000 intervals vs 32% for ERCOT Watches, 3.8 h lead; not better on precision, so no result

findings.who_loses: Nobody directly; the finding is about signal quality -- if the mechanical index does not clearly beat Watches, curated human/committee notices remain the best available public warning, which is itself informative (they are not obviously redundant with a simple slack calculation).
findings.software_fix: ERCOT / a third party: a real-time-computable, public net-load-slack index as a supplementary automated signal alongside Watch/EEA notices.

usd_scale.assumption: This finding is about signal quality (coverage/false-alarm/lead time), not a dollar transfer; no $ estimate is made or implied.

confidence.reason: Reuses established stats/watch.py + stats/tightness.py machinery and a vetted reserve-proxy series, but the underlying event counts are thin (a handful of $1000+ episodes and Watch windows per year) and eea_events.csv only has rows for 2021 and 2023 in this build, so per-year estimates are noisy even though the pooled bootstrap CI is reported honestly.

proxy_fields: reserve_proxy = nameplate dispatchable - net load (build/netload.py); NOT ERCOT's own Physical Responsive Capability

findings.title: ERCOT's own forecast beats the model where it exists
findings.claim: ERCOT's own slack forecast beats the model where it exists; the model adds value only where ERCOT's forecast is absent. Refitting stack on t2_headroom_lvl (expanding window) so it can actually see ERCOT's own isotonic-calibrated slack forecast as a model in its own right (the pre-refit comparison held that forecast out of a model that had never seen it), the baseline still scores 111% of the refit stack's Brier skill over climatology, pooled. By era, the baseline wins where ERCOT's own net-load forecast vintage is present in the row (post_2024 2.87x, rtc 4.06x) and the model only adds value where that vintage is structurally absent (pre_ecrs model 2.07x baseline, post_ecrs baseline BSS negative). Staleness caveat: Every ERCOT component behind this table and the settled wrapper ratio -- fc_load, fc_wind, fc_solar, fc_outage -- is sampled at 2 vintages/day (the archiver's current per_day setting), so the vintage available at the 10:00 CT decision cut has a median age of roughly 5 h for load/wind/solar and roughly 12 h for outage, not ERCOT's freshest posted vintage. slack_iso (and every *_fc_mw / slack_fc_mw / net_load_fc_mw quantity built on it) is therefore a STALE reconstruction of what ERCOT had published, not the freshest one -- the wrapper ratio compares the model against a deliberately hobbled version of ERCOT's own information, understating how good ERCOT's own forecast actually is at decision time. A fresh-vintage re-test (sampling near every product's 09:00-10:00 CT nearest vintage, >=4/day) is pending. See RESULTS.md S12.

headline.sub: [0.77, 1.70] 90% CI · >= 0.70 reframes as "adds X% on top of ERCOT's forecast" · stack · expanding · t2_headroom_lvl

confidence.reason: Pre-registered P2-WRAPPER line is 0.70 (baseline/model BSS over climatology); pooled wrapper ratio 1.11 [0.77, 1.70] clears it, so the headline is reframed as ERCOT's forecast plus a marginal model contribution, not a standalone model.
